ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: First describe the image: In the figure there are two vertical walls, hemispherical ball A is against the left wall, spherical ball B is against the right wall, and A and B are in contact with each other. The dashed line represents the line connecting the centers of the two balls, and this line has an included angle of 30° with the horizontal direction. B is in contact with the right wall, and A is in contact with the left wall. Then carry out force analysis: The spherical surface of B is smooth, so the force between A and B is along the line connecting the centers of the two balls. Let the magnitude of the supporting force of A on B be N. For force equilibrium of B, the mass of B is 2m, the gravitational force is 2mg, and the right wall only provides a horizontal supporting force, with no vertical friction. Equilibrium in the vertical direction gives N sin30° = 2mg, therefore N = 4mg. In the horizontal direction, the supporting force from the right wall balances N cos30°. Analyze A: The force of B on A is opposite to that of A on B, and its magnitude is still N; its vertical component is downward, with magnitude N sin30° = 2mg. A's own gravitational force is mg, therefore when A is just not sliding down, the maximum static friction force of the left wall on A is upward, with magnitude f = mg + 2mg = 3mg. The normal supporting force of the left wall on A is equal to the horizontal component of the force between A and B, namely N_A = N cos30° = 4mg × √3/2 = 2√3mg. Under the critical condition, the maximum static friction force is equal to the kinetic friction force, f = μN_A, so μ = 3mg / (2√3mg) = √3/2.
